records.reason: Results/Discussion compare the retested hug-eat verb pair with the 2013b study’s broader non-noun finding; that cited article is distinct from shipped row 391.
records.omission_quote: 6–9-month-olds did perform well on one of the two verb pairs ( hug - eat ), contrary to their poor performance on a broader set of non-nouns in a prior study ( Bergelson & Swingley, 2013 ). Whether infants’ apparent success on hug-eat represents random item variation, or a first fragile glimmer of infants’ understanding of these verbs, is unclear, particularly given infants’ failure to demonstrate understanding of kiss-drink here.
records.identity_quote: Bergelson E Swingley D The acquisition of abstract words by young infants. Cognition 2013b 127 3 391 7 doi:10.1016/j.cognition.2013.02.011

records.reason: Discussion expressly includes Parise & Csibra among earlier patterns confirmed and states that this new sample shows 6–9-month-olds understand words; cited EEG work is distinct from shipped row 391.
records.omission_quote: This study confirms several patterns that have emerged in previous work ( Bergelson & Swingley, 2012 , 2013b ; Parise & Csibra, 2012 ; Tincoff & Jusczyk, 1999 , 2012 ). Namely, we find further evidence, with a new sample of infants and a new set of item pairs, that 6-9 month olds understand words.
records.identity_quote: In an extension to EEG, Parise and Csibra (2012) demonstrated that 9-month-olds show an N400 mismatch effect when a revealed object (shown as a still image) does not match the word just uttered by infants’ mothers.

records.reason: The source describes Tincoff & Jusczyk (1999) as demonstrating Mommy/Daddy comprehension, but the present stimulus set has no proper-name pair; the citation is background to the broad early comprehension claim.
records.omission_quote: “Mommy” and “Daddy” were presented live on screen, and the “hand” and “feet” moved a bit in the image. While one video was named, infants’ eyegaze was measured; infants looked more at the matching video.
records.identity_quote: Tincoff R Jusczyk PW Some Beginnings of Word Comprehension in 6-Month-Olds. Psychological Science 1999 10 2 172 175 doi:10.1111/1467-9280.00127

records.reason: Current study explicitly retests the hand-feet pair previously tested by Tincoff & Jusczyk (2012). Shipped row 391 is the distinct Bergelson & Swingley (2012) work.
records.omission_quote: The words we tested had some overlap with previous work, but only one pair of nouns (hand-feet) had been tested before with young infants, as either still images or video clips ( Tincoff & Jusczyk, 2012 ).
records.identity_quote: These authors demonstrated that 6-month-olds understand two pairs of words: “hand” and “feet” (2012) and the proper names “Mommy” and “Daddy” (1999).

records.identity_quote: Lanovaz and Hranchuk (2021) trained models including the previous algorithm to identify changes in single-case AB graphs.

records.reason: Source explicitly says its multi-lab study re-tests the ACE version used in Borreggine & Kaschak (2006) and reports the replication result. Shipped row 519 is Glenberg & Kaschak (2002), a distinct earlier original.
records.omission_quote:
As a first step in assessing the replicability of motor
compatibility effects, we conducted a pre-registered, multi-lab
replication of the ACE. We used an adapted version of the
original ACE paradigm (Glenberg & Kaschak, 2002) that was
used in Borreggine and Kaschak (2006).
records.identity_quote: Borreggine, K. L., & Kaschak, M. P. (2006). The action–sentence compatibility effect: It's all in the timing. Cognitive Science, 30, 10971112.
